alerts.title: Rising creatinine on TDF in pregnancy
alerts.message: Guidelines list chronic kidney disease and Fanconi syndrome as TDF toxicities, with creatinine toxicity grading based on eGFR decline from baseline. Patient's creatinine rose from 0.8 to 1.1 mg/dL and eGFR fell from baseline to 78 mL/min/1.73m² after 10 weeks on TDF. This represents a >10% eGFR decline from baseline, meeting at least Grade 1 toxicity criteria. TDF is the likely contributor given the temporal relationship. Against drug attribution: pregnancy itself increases creatinine clearance demands, and 78 mL/min may partly reflect normal pregnancy-related physiology. Urinalysis is normal (no proteinuria, no glycosuria), and phosphate is normal, arguing against overt Fanconi syndrome. DTG can also affect tubular secretion but less commonly.

evidence.recommended_action: Continue TDF with close renal monitoring. Repeat creatinine/eGFR within 4 weeks. If progressive decline or proteinuria develops, consider switching to TAF-based regimen per guidelines.

alerts.title: Missing 6-month viral load monitoring plan
alerts.message: Guidelines state viral load should be measured 6 months after ART initiation and every 6–12 months or when clinically indicated. Patient initiated ART 10 weeks ago and already has a viral load of 89 copies/mL, which is encouraging. However, the formal 6-month VL is still due around month 6. No clinician plan was documented today, so it is unclear whether the 6-month VL has been scheduled. Additionally, CD4 monitoring should continue per schedule. The current VL of 89 copies/mL is suppressed but not undetectable; the 6-month VL will confirm sustained suppression.

evidence.recommended_action: Schedule the 6-month viral load test (approximately August 2026) and document a follow-up plan including ongoing CD4 and renal monitoring.

alerts.title: DTG hyperglycaemia screening gap in pregnancy
alerts.message: Guidelines require glucose screening before DTG initiation and glucose monitoring every 3 months for the first year in patients with risk factors for hyperglycaemia. Risk factors include BMI ≥25 kg/m². Patient's current weight is 68 kg; with pre-pregnancy weight of 62 kg and height unknown, BMI may exceed 25. No blood glucose result is documented. Pregnancy itself induces insulin resistance, compounding DTG's hyperglycaemia risk. Guidelines specify fasting glucose >6.95 mmol/L or non-fasting >8.89 mmol/L as thresholds for not initiating DTG. Without a documented glucose, hyperglycaemia risk is unassessed.

evidence.recommended_action: Check blood glucose now and repeat every 3 months during the first year of DTG therapy, given pregnancy and possible elevated BMI.

alerts.title: Anaemia and missing LFTs on ART
alerts.message: Guidelines list severe anaemia as a major toxicity of AZT and note that TDF toxicities require LFTs and RFTs when deranged. Patient's Hb is 10.8 g/dL, which is low for pregnancy (normal cutoff ≥11 g/dL). She is not on AZT, so anaemia is not drug-attributable to her current regimen. However, no cause has been investigated. She takes ferrous sulfate and folic acid, suggesting pre-existing iron deficiency or prophylactic use. Pregnancy-related haemodilution and iron deficiency are the most likely causes. Baseline Hb was not provided, so trend cannot be assessed. LFTs have not been documented despite 10 weeks on ART.

evidence.recommended_action: Investigate anaemia with iron studies and reticulocyte count. Perform LFTs as part of routine ART toxicity monitoring.
